chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ali ibn al-Rayyan, from Yunus, who said:

I asked Al-Khurasani (peace be upon him) and said, 'Indeed, Al-Abbasi mentioned that you allow regarding singing (music).' He said, 'The apostate has lied! I did not say to him like this. He asked me about singing, so I said to him, 'A man came to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) and asked him about singing. He said, 'O so-and-so, if Allah differentiates between the Truth and the Falsehood, where would singing be?' He said, 'With the Falsehood.' He said, 'So you have judged.'

key_terms.أَبُو جَعْفَرٍ: Abu Ja'far (Imam al-Sadiq, peace be upon him)
key_terms.الزِّنِدِيقُ: The apostate or heretic (referring to Al-Abbasi)
key_terms.الْغِنَاءُ: Singing or music, specifically melodic vocal performance

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on singing (ghina') in Shia Islam according to Imam al-Rida?
ai.summary: Imam al-Rida (peace be upon him) clarifies that his stance on singing was not a blanket permissibility but a logical deduction based on Imam al-Sadiq’s (peace be upon him) rhetorical question linking it to falsehood. This narration highlights the Shia scholarly method of deriving rulings through contextual reasoning rather than rigid literalism, emphasizing that singing is inherently tied to the realm of *al-batil* (falsehood) when distinguished from truth. The refutation of the Abbasid claim underscores the precision required in interpreting juristic statements within their specific historical and intellectual contexts.
